questions.q: What is the reaction in which Fe<sup>2+</sup> accepts electrons called (oxidation or reduction)?
What is the oxidation reaction of H<sub>2</sub> (g)?

Does a reaction take place between Fe<sup>2+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub> (g)? (use BINAS table 48)
questions.a: No. Fe<sup>2+</sup> is the oxidising agent and in BINAS table 48 it is below the reducing agent H<sub>2</sub> (g), so no reaction takes place. Or: the difference in electrode potential is −0.45 volt, so no energy can be released; it costs energy to make this reaction happen.

questions.q: Does a reaction take place between copper(II) sulfate and the metal aluminium? (use BINAS table 48)
questions.a: Cu<sup>2+</sup> is the oxidising agent and in BINAS table 48 it is above the reducing agent Al (s). So yes.

questions.a: Noble metals: Au and Ag; base metals: zinc, iron, aluminium; very reactive metals: lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium

questions.q: Define corrosion
questions.a: Attack on metals by a redox reaction with substances from the air, especially oxygen, water and acids

questions.q: Why do many base metals not corrode away completely?
questions.a: They react in such a way that a metal oxide or metal hydroxide layer forms that is impermeable, so the corrosion stops

questions.q: Why does iron rust away completely?
questions.a: A porous oxide/hydroxide layer forms, so the corrosion continues and the rust flakes off

questions.q: Which two kinds of protection of metals against corrosion exist?
Name an active method of protecting a metal
questions.a: Galvanising. Applying a layer of another metal.

questions.q: Name a passive method of protecting a metal
questions.a: Coating or painting with lacquer or plastic

questions.q: Name two ways of galvanising.
questions.a: Dipping in a liquid metal; applying a layer of metal electrochemically

questions.q: Can you galvanise with a more reactive metal?
questions.a: Yes, for example a zinc layer on iron. Zinc itself forms a thin layer of zinc oxide that protects both the zinc underneath and the iron

questions.q: How do noble, base and very reactive metals differ in chemical/redox terms?
questions.a: The stronger a reducing agent the metal is, the more reactive (less noble) it is

questions.q: In salt water corrosion goes faster because it conducts current; how can we protect steel ships against corrosion? Explain.
questions.a: By attaching sacrificial metal: zinc blocks fitted to the steel hull; because iron is slightly more noble than zinc, the zinc will corrode away first and only then the iron

questions.q: What is an electrochemical cell? Explain.
questions.a: A set-up in which the oxidation and reduction reactions take place separately, so that electrons can flow through a wire to power electrical devices, e.g. a lamp

questions.q: Which metals are used in a Daniell cell? What is the reducing agent and what is the oxidising agent?
questions.a: Copper, the oxidising agent is Cu<sup>2+</sup>; zinc, the reducing agent is Zn (s)

questions.q: Which metal seems to disappear in a Daniell cell and which one grows?
questions.a: Zinc seems to disappear, it dissolves as Zn<sup>2+</sup>; copper seems to appear out of nowhere

questions.q: Which metal is the + and which the − electrode in a Daniell cell?
questions.a: Zinc is the − electrode, it donates electrons; copper is the + electrode, it passes the electrons on to the copper ions in the solution

questions.q: What is a salt bridge and why is it needed in an electrochemical cell?
questions.a: A salt bridge is a connection between the reducing-agent and the oxidising-agent solutions, needed to balance the flow of electrons so that the total charge transfer is zero. E.g. a gel with KCl or NaCl

questions.q: Are there inert electrodes? What are they, and if so, do you know one?
questions.a: Yes, for example platinum or carbon electrodes; they do not take part in the chemical reaction that occurs, they only conduct the electric current
